title: Wild ginger (jidu)

names.gloss: wild ginger, Scott's ginger; its fruit is ripe in March
native ginger with fruit ripe March–May

identification.basis: Roth's Bloomfield plant list gives jeddo for Elettaria scottiana, now Hornstedtia scottiana, Scott's ginger, still called jiddo in English; the dictionary has jidu and junjun, the latter Roth's Amomum dallachyi. Anderson records wild-ginger leaves as the earth-oven flavouring and the leaching trough.

summary: **[jidu](word:jidu)** is the wild ginger, Scott's ginger, *Hornstedtia scottiana*, which Roth wrote as *jeddo* and English still calls jiddo: a big ginger 'about 2–4 m tall' with the flowers and the red fruit 'raised only slightly above ground level' at its base, in the lowland rainforest of the Bloomfield and Daintree [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:roth1901] [ref:rfkginger]. Its leaves are the kitchen's foil: at Bloomfield the meat went into the [earth oven](entry:earth-oven) 'with *Eucalyptus*, *Acacia* or wild ginger leaves for flavouring'; the Bloomfield ovens were lined with 'various species of ginger'; the *junda* nut cakes were 'wrapped up in wild-ginger leaves, and baked in the ashes'; the Tully people baked green-ant larvae 'rolled up, in the dry, in "wild-ginger" leaves'; and the small fish of the flood run were 'tied up in wild-ginger leaves ready for baking' [ref:anderson1996] [ref:roth1901]. The leaves also made the trough that led water into the [leaching](entry:leaching) bag, and the fruit is eaten and feeds the cassowary [ref:anderson1996] [ref:rfkginger]. This is a plant of the Eastern Kuku Yalanji rainforest, the Bloomfield and Daintree coast; it is on this page because the words, the trade and the tools reach inland. Each place below says what grows there.

sections.heading: Names
sections.body: **[jidu](word:jidu)** and **[junjun](word:junjun)** are the dictionary's gingers: *jidu* with fruit ripe in March, and *junjun* 'a rainforest plant with fruit ripe in March to May', which Roth identified as *Amomum dallachyi*; the scrub turkey, the dictionary says, comes down to the *junjun* in its season [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:roth1901]. Roth's Bloomfield name for *Elettaria scottiana*, now *Hornstedtia scottiana*, was *jeddo*; the rainforest key gives 'Scott's ginger; jiddo; native cardamom' as its common names [ref:roth1901] [ref:rfkginger].

sections.heading: The plant and its uses
sections.body:
'Usually flowers and fruits as a shrubby plant about 2–4 m tall but it should be noted that only the leaves are above ground level. The true stem is below the soil surface.' 'Inflorescences produced on short shoots from the base of the plant and are raised only slightly above ground level ... sterile bracts often bright red'. 'Grows as an understory shrub in disturbed areas in lowland rain forest', from near sea level to 200 m, on Cape York and in the Wet Tropics; 'fruit eaten by cassowaries' [ref:rfkginger].

**In the oven.** Anderson's Bloomfield informants: 'the meat, along with *Eucalyptus*, *Acacia* or wild ginger leaves for flavouring, was then put into a bark trough which was placed on the rocks in the hole' [ref:anderson1996]. Roth: the Bloomfield ovens were lined with 'various species of ginger'; the *Pygeum* nut, *junda*, pounded and sifted, was 'kneaded into cakes, wrapped up in wild-ginger leaves, and baked in the ashes'; on the Tully the green-ant larvae were 'rolled up, in the dry, in "wild-ginger" leaves and baked', and the fry taken in the flood were 'tied up in wild-ginger leaves ready for baking' [ref:roth1901]. In the yam processing, 'with the help of leaves [pandanus or wild ginger] acting as a trough, water is allowed to' run into the bag [ref:anderson1996].

sections.heading: Ginger, cardamom, lily
sections.body:
- **Scott's ginger** (*jidu*): tall leafy shoots, the red-bracted flowers and the fruit at the base, a ginger smell when the leaf is crushed [ref:rfkginger].
- ***Amomum*** (*junjun*): another ginger of the same scrubs, fruit March to May [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:roth1901].
- **Cunjevoi and the big arum lilies**: broad leaves, no ginger smell, and poisonous; see [leaching](entry:leaching) [ref:palmer1883].
- **Paperbark** is the inland wrapping; see [paperbark](entry:paperbark) [ref:anderson1996].

sections.heading: Signs
sections.body:
- **A clump of leafy shoots** taller than a person in a rainforest gap [ref:rfkginger].
- **Red bracts at ground level** at the base of the clump, and the fruit after [ref:rfkginger].
- **Cassowary droppings** with ginger seed [ref:rfkginger].
- **Scrub turkeys** down in the *junjun* in its season [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: Where it grows
sections.body: 'Disturbed areas in lowland rain forest', from near sea level to 200 m, on Cape York and in the Wet Tropics [ref:rfkginger].

sections.heading: The oven leaf
sections.body: Wild ginger is the rainforest kitchen's leaf: lining, wrapping, flavouring and trough, around the [earth oven](entry:earth-oven), the [leaching](entry:leaching) pits and the ashes; its fruit feeds the [cassowary](entry:cassowary) and the [scrub turkey](entry:scrub-turkey) and people in March [ref:anderson1996] [ref:roth1901] [ref:rfkginger] [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: Seasons
sections.body: Fruit in March (*jidu*) and March to May (*junjun*), the end of the wet; leaves all year [ref:hershberger1982]. See [the year on country](entry:seasons).

sections.heading: Uses
sections.body:
- Flavouring and lining in the earth oven [ref:anderson1996] [ref:roth1901].
- Wrapping for nut cakes, fish and ant larvae baked in the ashes [ref:roth1901].
- A leaf trough for leaching water [ref:anderson1996].
- Fruit eaten [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:rfkginger].

sections.heading: Cooking in ginger leaves
sections.body:
From Roth and Anderson [ref:roth1901] [ref:anderson1996]:

1. **Cut the big leaves** from the clump; they are long and tough enough to tie [ref:rfkginger].
2. **Line the oven** with them under the meat, and lay more over it, with gum and wattle leaves if you want that flavour [ref:anderson1996] [ref:roth1901].
3. **Wrap small things**: a cake of pounded nut, a handful of fry, a ball of ant larvae, tied up in a leaf and put in the ashes [ref:roth1901].
4. **Make a trough** of leaves to lead water from a stream into a leaching bag [ref:anderson1996].
5. The [earth oven](entry:earth-oven) page has the whole method.

sections.heading: Safety
sections.body:
- Know the ginger by its smell; the broad-leaved arums of the same gullies are poisonous raw [ref:palmer1883].
- Rainforest gullies are cassowary country; see [cassowary](entry:cassowary).

sections.heading: On Country today
sections.body: Wild ginger is gathered on someone's country: each place below says whose.

sections.heading: Language
sections.body: *[jidu](word:jidu)* wild ginger; *[junjun](word:junjun)* a ginger with fruit ripe March–May [ref:hershberger1982].

locations.summary: **No wild ginger is recorded on the Hann.** The Atlas of Living Australia holds no record of any plant of the ginger family in a box of about 90 × 85 km around the middle Hann, Laura and western Rinyirru [ref:ala-hann], and Scott's ginger is a plant of lowland rainforest [ref:rfkginger]. Around Princess Charlotte Bay, Roth's 'wild ginger' was a different plant, the native turmeric *Curcuma australasica*, eaten for its roots [ref:roth1901].

sections.heading: Not on the Hann
sections.body: Along the Hann grow 'stringybark, bloodwood, Moreton Bay ash and ironbark trees with a ground cover of coarse grasses such as speargrass' [ref:wp-hann], with a paperbark fringe on the big streams [ref:qld-re]. The closest thing to rainforest in this country is closed forest and vine thicket, 'very restricted' in Rinyirru [ref:qpws-rinyirru-2013], and the Atlas box holds no ginger of any kind [ref:ala-hann].

sections.heading: Ginger and oven leaves here
sections.body:
**Wild ginger of the Bay.** Roth lists *Curcuma australasica* as '"Wild ginger"': 'Tuberous roots either roasted or boiled', with names in the Koko-rarmul and Koko-wara languages of Princess Charlotte Bay [ref:roth1901]. It is a root food, not an oven leaf, and the Atlas has no record of it near the Hann either [ref:ala-hann].

**Covering the oven.** No published record says what leaves the people of the Hann laid in an earth oven. On the Morehead River, which runs like the Hann to Princess Charlotte Bay, Roth saw yams 'baked in a hot ant-bed covered with tea-tree bark and earth' [ref:roth1901]. See [paperbark](entry:paperbark) and [earth oven](entry:earth-oven).

locations.summary: [Karma Waters](place:karma-waters) on the upper Mitchell is a long way from the ginger's rainforest. The river at Karma Waters has no wild ginger; the [paperbark](entry:paperbark) is the wrapping there.

sections.heading: Not here
sections.body: Wild ginger grows in lowland rainforest [ref:rfkginger], not the dry woodland of the upper Mitchell.

locations.summary: This is jidu's country: the Bloomfield and Daintree scrubs and creek gullies, where it is the oven leaf [ref:rfkginger] [ref:anderson1996].

sections.heading: Where it grows here
sections.body: 'Disturbed areas in lowland rain forest': the Bloomfield and Daintree scrubs and creek gullies [ref:rfkginger].

sections.heading: On country today
sections.body: Jiddo grows in the Bloomfield scrubs and is still the oven leaf; the Eastern Kuku Yalanji country it grows on was handed back in 2021 [ref:rfkginger] [ref:handback2021].
